prompt: Order the three topics that Sprint Planning addresses, as described in the Scrum Guide 2020.

task.prompt: Drag the items into the right order, first at the top.

items.label: What can be Done this Sprint? (select backlog items)
Why is this Sprint valuable? (craft the Sprint Goal)
How will the chosen work get done? (plan the work, often into tasks of a day or less)

task.explanation: The Scrum Guide 2020 lists Topic One (why, the Sprint Goal), Topic Two (what) and Topic Three (how).

prompt: Plan a 2-week (10 working day) sprint. Each person has 6 focus hours per day for sprint work. Work out the team's hours available for sprint work.

task.prompt: Calculate each value from the data.
task.explanation: Available days × 6 h: Asha 10×6=60, Ben 8×6=48, Chen 10×6=60, Dana 9×6=54. Total = 222 hours.

prompt: Your team's last three sprints completed the points below. Next sprint one of the five developers is off for 4 of 10 days. Use the average velocity scaled by availability to suggest how many points to plan.

task.prompt: Calculate each value from the data.

fields.label: Suggested points for next sprint (avg × availability)

prompt: Here is a draft sprint plan for a client's e-commerce app. Mark the parts that break good sprint-planning practice.

task.prompt: Mark every segment that is a problem. Leave the sound ones unmarked.

segments.text: Sprint Goal: Shoppers can pay by card and see an order confirmation.
Selected: 6 stories totalling 31 points; our 3-sprint average is 30.
Also selected: 12 more 'stretch' stories (40 points) so the client sees we're ambitious.
segments.issue: Loading far beyond proven velocity sets up a failed sprint and false client expectations.

segments.text: Payment gateway story has no acceptance criteria yet; we'll work them out during the sprint.
segments.issue: Items pulled in should be ready; no acceptance criteria means the team cannot know when it is Done.

segments.text: The PM assigned every task to named developers before the meeting.
segments.issue: Developers plan how to do the work and choose who does it; pre-assigning removes their ownership.

segments.text: Dana's 2 days of leave are subtracted from capacity.
We'll review progress at each Daily Scrum against the Sprint Goal.

prompt: Halfway through Sprint Planning on a fixed-bid marketplace project, the client's product owner asks to add a 'refer a friend' feature (estimated 13 points) to this sprint. The selected work already matches your average velocity.

task.prompt: Halfway through Sprint Planning on a fixed-bid marketplace project, the client's product owner asks to add a 'refer a friend' feature (estimated 13 points) to this sprint. The selected work already matches your average velocity.

steps.question: What do you do in the meeting?
options: Add it and ask the team to work weekends
Explain the sprint is full; offer to swap it for work of similar size or put it at the top of the backlog for next sprint
Add it silently and drop testing to fit
steps.explanation: The PO can trade scope, but adding 13 points on top of a full sprint just breaks the forecast.

steps.question: The PO also confirms the feature was not in the signed scope. What else is needed?
options: Nothing, agile means scope is free
Raise a change request so its cost and timeline impact on the fixed bid are agreed
steps.explanation: On a fixed bid, new scope needs a change request before it is built, even if prioritised in the backlog.

prompt: Order these Sprint Planning steps for a mature team.

task.prompt: Drag the items into the right order, first at the top.

items.label: Developers select items that fit capacity and support the goal
PO presents the objective and top-ordered, refined backlog items
Developers break selected items into tasks and check the plan is realistic

task.explanation: Knowing capacity first keeps selection honest; the goal guides selection; tasks come last as the 'how'.

prompt: In the middle of a sprint, the developers discover the 'export to CSV' story is three times bigger than estimated. The Sprint Goal (launch the admin dashboard) does not depend on it.

task.prompt: In the middle of a sprint, the developers discover the 'export to CSV' story is three times bigger than estimated. The Sprint Goal (launch the admin dashboard) does not depend on it.

steps.question: What is the right response?
options: Developers and PO renegotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog, e.g. move the story back to the Product Backlog
Change the Sprint Goal to 'export to CSV'
steps.explanation: The Scrum Guide lets scope be clarified and renegotiated with the PO as more is learned, as long as the Sprint Goal is not endangered.

steps.question: What should you take into the next Sprint Planning?
options: Re-estimate the story with what was learned and split it if possible
steps.explanation: Use the new knowledge: re-estimate and split so it fits a sprint.

prompt: What is the maximum length of Sprint Planning for a one-month sprint, according to the Scrum Guide?

mcq.explanation: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint; shorter Sprints usually take less.

prompt: Who selects how many Product Backlog items go into the sprint?

options: The PM, based on the contract
mcq.explanation: The Product Owner orders the backlog and explains it, but the Developers select how much they can do because they are the ones accountable for the work.

prompt: A client asks why the team commits to a Sprint Goal instead of to every story selected. What is the best explanation?

options: The goal gives a single objective and lets the team flex the detailed scope as they learn, while still delivering value
Stories are never finished in Scrum
Goals are only for internal use
The Scrum Guide forbids selecting stories
mcq.explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog; it gives focus and flexibility on the exact work needed to reach it.
